one_liner: CPython plus NumPy and SciPy compiled to WebAssembly; one informal test inverted a 200x200 matrix about 20x faster than math.js.
what_it_does: Pyodide is CPython ported to WebAssembly with Emscripten, running in browsers and Node.js. It adds a JavaScript-Python foreign function interface and micropip, and ships prebuilt ports of C, C++ and Rust packages such as NumPy, pandas, SciPy, Matplotlib and scikit-learn. You call loadPyodide() from pyodide.mjs (jsDelivr CDN or npm), load packages, then run Python code or call Python functions through proxies. It does not replace math.js as a drop-in: you write the maths in Python with NumPy and move data across the FFI.
how_it_is_fast: The speedup comes from NumPy's compiled C, not from anything Pyodide adds. np.linalg.inv copies the matrix into a contiguous buffer and calls LAPACK gesv (LU with partial pivoting) against an identity matrix. Pyodide builds NumPy with -Dallow-noblas=true and no BLAS dependency, so gesv runs NumPy's f2c-translated lapack_lite reference code (NumPy calls these '(slow!) internal fallback routines'), compiled by Emscripten at -O2 with no blocking, SIMD or threads. math.js's inv does Gauss-Jordan elimination over nested JS arrays and sends every scalar step through typed-function dispatch: about 12 million addScalar(multiply()) steps for a 200x200 matrix (derived from inv.js). The gap therefore measures that dispatch overhead, not WebAssembly against JavaScript.
when_to_use: Browser or Node.js apps that need real NumPy, SciPy or pandas behaviour on the client (notebooks, teaching tools, offline data apps) when the alternative is rewriting the numerics in JavaScript.
Dense linear algebra on matrices of a few hundred rows where math.js's generic matrices are the incumbent: 0.024 s vs 0.475 s (Chrome) for one 200x200 inverse.
Long-lived sessions where the multi-megabyte download and the seconds of startup are paid once, run in a module Web Worker so synchronous Python does not block the UI.
Porting existing Python numerical code to the web with little rewriting.
when_not_to_use: One-off or latency-sensitive page loads: the roadmap cites a 6.4 MB first download and 4 to 5 s of initialization for the core, and NumPy adds about 2.8 MB compressed (issue #3763). The comparison measured none of this.

Heavy BLAS-3 work: Pyodide's reference BLAS ran dgemm 15-35x slower than native (issue #3763), a 1024x1024 float32 np.dot took about 3 s vs 0.005 s natively (issue #1574), and native NumPy did the 200x200 inverse 2.7x faster than Pyodide.
Data that lives in JavaScript: every array has to cross the JS-Python FFI (issue #2232 reports costly NumPy-to-tfjs transfers). The benchmark avoided this cost by generating its data inside Python.
Multithreaded work: threading, multiprocessing and subprocess raise RuntimeError (FAQ).
A single kernel such as a matrix product or an inverse, where a typed-array JS library or a small Emscripten or Rust wasm module needs far less code and download.

integration.form: module (JavaScript loader pyodide.mjs plus the pyodide.asm.wasm runtime, python_stdlib.zip and per-package wheels, from the jsDelivr CDN or npm)
integration.dependencies: none for the runtime; NumPy and other packages load separately as wheels through loadPackage or micropip
integration.min_toolchain: Node.js 18+ (npm engines field) or a modern browser with WebAssembly; current main builds Python 3.14.2 with Emscripten 5.0.3; Web Workers must be module-type
integration.platforms: wasm32 in browsers and Node.js; no pthreads
integration.thread_safety: Single-threaded: threading, multiprocessing and subprocess raise RuntimeError; run Pyodide in a module Web Worker to keep the main thread responsive.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it replaces math.js only if you rewrite the maths as Python/NumPy calls behind the FFI; there is no math.js-compatible API

gotchas: The evidence is one informal post (dvd101x, math.js discussion #2744, 2023-02-11). It gives no machine, browser versions, Pyodide or math.js version, run count or warm-up, and every timed expression includes generating the random matrix. The stable Pyodide release on that date was 0.22.1 (2023-01-25), whose NumPy 1.23.5 recipe was built with --disable-optimization.

The 20x mostly measures math.js's generic typed-function dispatch: a math.js maintainer named that indirection as the main cause of its slowness in December 2024, and math.js ran 5x slower in Safari than in Chrome. It is not a WebAssembly-vs-JavaScript result: native NumPy is still 2.7x faster than Pyodide on the same inverse, and no plain typed-array JavaScript loop was measured.

Pyodide's NumPy has no optimized BLAS or LAPACK. It uses the lapack_lite fallback, the OpenBLAS evaluation (issue #3763, open since 2023-04) has not landed, and a NumPy maintainer said in that issue that NumPy is considering dropping lapack-lite, so large matrices fall far behind native.
Releases are now numbered after the Python version (314.0.7 on 2026-09-14, with 0.29.x and 0.27.x stable branches). Compiled packages must be built for the matching Pyodide ABI.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Pyodide over single-kernel siblings such as wasm-perf (Emscripten SIMD matmul) or the Rust matmul in JavaScript-vs-WebAssembly-Comparative-Analysis when you need the whole Python scientific stack rather than one hand-written routine. Pick those siblings, or a typed-array JS library, when you need one operation with a small download and no interpreter startup.
verified_claims_summary: One informal timing in math.js discussion #2744 (2023-02-11; machine, browser versions and run counts not stated): inverting a freshly generated random 200x200 matrix took 0.024 s with NumPy in Pyodide in the browser, 0.475 s with math.js in Chrome (about 20x, derived from page data) and 2.403 s with math.js in Safari. Native NumPy on Python 3.10 took 0.009 s and Octave 0.005 s. Download and initialization time were not included.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-22, 14.9k stars, MPL-2.0, latest release 314.0.7 on 2026-09-14) and widely used. The only performance evidence is a third-party anecdote that pits NumPy's compiled reference LAPACK against math.js's generic dispatch, and the category fit is loose because Pyodide is a Python runtime, not a wasm language.
